The belief goes like this: marking a method
makes it run in the background, on a new or separate thread, so the caller is never held up. Calling it starts a parallel job, and
waits for that job to finish.
It's an easy model to arrive at. "Asynchronous" sounds like "at the same time." Before

often runs on a different thread than the code before it, which looks like proof.
But Microsoft's docs say it plainly: the
keywords don't cause extra threads to be created. The thread you see after an
was borrowed, and the code before the first real wait never left the caller's thread.

it reached. Calling the method starts that state machine right away, on the calling thread, like any other call. It keeps running there until it awaits something that isn't finished yet. A method that never reaches such an
runs synchronously from start to end, whatever its signature says.

, the method first checks whether the awaited task has already completed. If it has, the method takes the result and keeps going without pausing. If not, it registers the rest of the method as a
, saves its state, and returns. In Release builds this is the moment the state machine, a struct until now, is copied to the heap. The caller receives an unfinished
and carries on, or awaits it and returns to its own caller in turn. On a UI thread, that return is what lets the window keep processing clicks and repainting.
While it waits, no thread waits with it

Suppose the awaited operation is an HTTP request or a database query. Once the request is on its way, there's nothing to execute until the response arrives, so no thread of yours sits blocked on it. That's the whole point on a server: ASP.NET Core can serve thousands of concurrent requests with a small pool of threads, because those threads aren't parked waiting for I/O.
Where the rest of the method runs
When the awaited task completes, the continuation needs some thread to run on. By default,

Over its lifetime, one async method can run on several threads, one after another, but never on two at once. None of those threads exists because you wrote
